questions.prompt: Which statement best describes what "web performance" covers?

options.text: Only how long the page takes to finish loading
Loading, rendering, and how responsive the page is to input after it loads
How visually attractive the design is
The number of features the site has

questions.explanation: Web performance spans loading (getting the bytes), rendering (turning them into pixels), and runtime responsiveness (reacting to taps, clicks, and scrolling) — not just the initial load time.

questions.prompt: Which statements about PERCEIVED performance are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: It is how fast the experience feels to the user
It can be improved without changing the raw timings (e.g. with skeletons and instant feedback)
Reserving space so content doesn't jump can improve it
It is exactly the same thing as the total load time

questions.explanation: Perceived performance is the subjective sense of speed; progressive rendering, instant tap feedback, and reserving space all improve it even if raw timings are unchanged. It is not identical to total load time.

questions.prompt: In the RAIL model, the letter "R" stands for ____ — handling user input quickly.
questions.explanation: RAIL stands for Response, Animation, Idle, and Load. Response is about handling user interactions fast enough that they feel immediate.

questions.prompt: Order these phases as a user experiences them for a fresh page view, from first to last.

items.text: The page reacts to a tap or click (runtime responsiveness)

questions.explanation: At a high level the browser must receive bytes, render them into visible pixels, and only then can the loaded page respond to interaction.

questions.prompt: Match each RAIL goal to what it is about.

pairs.right: Handle user input quickly so it feels immediate
Produce each frame fast enough to stay smooth
Do non-urgent work in small chunks during idle time

questions.explanation: RAIL frames the experience from the user's side: respond to input fast, animate smoothly, use idle time in small pieces, and load meaningful content quickly.

questions.prompt: Whose experience should you primarily optimize for?

options.text: Your own fast laptop on a fast office network
The single fastest visit ever recorded
A realistic 75th-percentile user, often on a mid-range phone and mobile network

questions.explanation: A fast dev machine hides the CPU and network costs real users pay. Optimizing for the 75th-percentile real user (typically mobile) reflects what most people actually experience.
